lesson.title: Numbers & the Four-Twenties
lesson.subtitle: Counting 1–100, vigesimal quatre-vingts ('four score'), and expressing age as possession with avoir

hook.title: Why French Counts Like the Gettysburg Address
hook.content: When Abraham Lincoln opened the Gettysburg Address with 'Four score and seven years ago', a 'score' meant twenty — so four score and seven was 4 × 20 + 7 = 87. Standard French still counts its 70s, 80s, and 90s using that ancient Celtic/Norman twenty-based (vigesimal) system! Up to sixty (soixante) everything is decimal. Then at 70, instead of inventing a new ten-word, French says soixante-dix ('sixty-ten'). At 80 it says quatre-vingts ('four-twenties'). And at 90 it says quatre-vingt-dix ('four-twenty-ten')!

footnotes.title: How every number from 1 to 10 hides inside English
footnotes.content: un (unit), deux (duet/deuce), trois (trio/three), quatre (quartet), cinq (quintet), six (six), sept (September), huit (octopus/October), neuf (November), dix (decimal), vingt (vigesimal), cent (century/percent).

pattern.title: You Don't 'Be' Your Age in French — You 'Have' Your Years
pattern.content: In English you say 'I am thirty years old', treating age as an identity. In French, years are something you collect and carry in your pocket with avoir: J'ai trente ans (literally 'I have thirty years'). And you never drop the word ans ('years'): English can say 'I am thirty', but French always names the years: J'ai vingt ans, il a quarante ans.
pattern.linguist_note: Gaulish substratum counting by twenties (vigesimal) survived in Parisian French for 70–99, while Swiss and Belgian French regularized them to septante, huitante/octante, and nonante.
pattern.trap_note: The shortcut your mind will offer: saying *Je suis trente ans for 'I am thirty years old'. Age is possession in Romance: ALWAYS use avoir (J'ai trente ans)!

exercises.prompt: Match each French number with its English cognate clue and value:
exercises.explanation: 70 adds dix onto soixante; 80 multiplies quatre × vingt.

exercises.prompt: What is the literal word-for-word structure of 'J'ai trente ans'?
exercises.meaning: Literal structure: I have thirty years
exercises.explanation: French expresses age as possession with avoir: J'ai trente ans ('I have thirty years').

exercises.prompt: French cent ('100') and ans ('years') combine inside which English word for a 100-year period?
exercises.explanation: Latin centum ('hundred') gave French cent and English century / percent.

exercises.idea: my brother is twenty years old
cues: has twenty years → a vingt ans (use avoir, not est!)
exercises.meaning: My brother is twenty years old
exercises.explanation: Mon frère a vingt ans uses il a ('has') + vingt ans.

diagnosis.slip: used est instead of a for age
diagnosis.cue: Age uses avoir: Mon frère a vingt ans.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.meaning: I am thirty years old today
exercises.explanation: trente ans links with a /t/ liaison (/tʁɑ̃.t‿ɑ̃/).
exercises.affirmation: You used J'ai + ans and spelled aujourd'hui with its apostrophe.

summary.outcome: Count from 1 to 100 including vigesimal 70–99, and state ages using avoir + ans.

use_example.german: Mon père a soixante ans et j'ai trente ans.
use_example.english: My father is sixty and I am thirty.

summary.takeaway: 80 is four-twenties (quatre-vingts), and you always 'have' your years (j'ai X ans).

twist.prompt: Ungraded — ask a friend 'How old are you?' (literally 'Which age have you?' using Quel âge):
twist.explanation: Because you 'have' your age, 'How old are you?' is Tu as quel âge ? (or Quel âge as-tu ?).

deux.etymology_derivation: Latin duo — English duo, deuce (the two-card).

trois.etymology_derivation: Latin trēs and English three share the Proto-Indo-European *treyes — the oldest cognate pair on the trail.

quatre.etymology_derivation: Latin quattuor — quartet, quarter. And quatre-vingts is four twenties: the count of 'four score'.

cinq.etymology_derivation: Latin quinque — quintet, quintessence (the fifth element).

six.etymology_derivation: Final x sounds like /s/ alone, is silent before a consonant (six jours /si ʒuʁ/), and buzzes as /z/ before a vowel (six ans /si.z‿ɑ̃/).

sept.etymology_derivation: Latin septem — September was month seven of the old calendar before January butted in.

huit.shift_rule: Latin octō, o breathed into hu-
huit.etymology_derivation: Latin octō — octopus, October. French breathed an h in front: huit.

neuf.etymology_derivation: Latin novem 'nine' — November, the ninth month. The same word (from novus) also means new.

vingt.etymology_derivation: Latin vīgintī — English 'vigesimal' (counting by twenties) is the same root; French just kept counting that way: quatre-vingts.

quatre_vingts.etymology_derivation: Literally 'four-twenties', just like Abraham Lincoln's 'four score'. And 90 is quatre-vingt-dix ('four-twenty-ten')!

ans.context_translation: I'm thirty years old (I have thirty years).
ans.etymology_derivation: Latin annus — annual, anniversary. Age is something you have in French: j'ai X ans.
